I’ve been farming these fields in Quzhou for more than forty years. The land here is flat, the soil is loamy, and the water table is still good enough for a few rounds of irrigation. I know this place season by season. I’m sixty‑eight now—my back isn’t what it used to be—so I don’t chase risky crops. I stick to the rotation that always puts food on the table and leaves a little cash in my pocket: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That’s the double‑cropping system every household around here relies on.

This year I have eight mu of good arable land. I’ll plant all eight mu to improved wheat in late autumn. Wheat is our staple; my family eats the flour, and the surplus sells easily to the grain station. I’ll rotary‑till the plots to break up the stubble and make a fine seedbed. I’ll put down compound fertilizer as a basal dose and top‑dress with urea in the spring. Wheat needs water at key stages, so I’ll irrigate four times: the critical winter irrigation, plus three more times at green‑up, jointing, and grain‑filling. I’ll spray for weeds, aphids, and fungal diseases about four times total—herbicide once early, then insecticide and fungicide as the weather dictates. I expect roughly 1,100 kg per mu if the spring rains cooperate.

As soon as the wheat comes off the combine in early June, I’ll sow hybrid maize directly into the stubble with no‑tillage. There’s no time to waste between the two crops, and no‑tillage saves fuel, labor, and precious soil moisture. Maize is less hungry for fertilizer than wheat, but it still needs nitrogen to push the big ears. I’ll irrigate twice—once at the V6 stage and again at tasseling/silking—and spray pesticides three or four times to control corn borers and leaf blight. With a decent summer, I should get about 1,150 kg per mu of grain.

That’s my plan. It’s not fancy, but it’s steady. I know these crops, the buyers know these crops, and at my age that predictability matters more than gambling on something new.
